notes: Each eval points the skill at a real graph-based system and asks for its guide. Expectations assert on evidence honesty, content coverage and proportionate process — not on wording or section order, since two competent runs will structure a guide differently and both be right. The load-bearing expectations are the negative ones: no invented security controls, no declared behavior narrated as observed, no silent omission of an area the evidence does not support. Evals 3 and 4 exist because the cheapest way to fail this specification is to over-process a small job or to regenerate a document that only needed a patch.

evals.name: full-guide-from-repo-only-evidence
evals.prompt: We're onboarding a new maintainer onto our agent pipeline next week and there is no documentation at all. Can you write a proper architecture and operations guide for it? Everything's in this repo — the graph is in src/graph.py, prompts under prompts/, and the deploy stuff is in deploy/. Put it in docs/. There's no staging access from here so you can only go off the code.
evals.expected_output: A guide in docs/ covering all thirteen content areas or marking them not applicable with a reason, with claims labeled declared/observed/inferred/unknown, a source register recording what was inspected and at which revision, and a verification summary naming unresolved gaps.
expectations: The guide covers every required content area, or explicitly marks an area not applicable with a stated reason — no area is silently dropped.
Claims are labeled by evidence state, and behavior read from code, config or prompts is labeled declared rather than presented as observed.
Deployment is labeled declared (read from infrastructure files), and the guide states that the running environment was not inspected.
The security section names only controls traceable to inspected files, and reports verified gaps where a control a reader would expect is absent.
No security control is asserted generically (no unsupported 'encrypted at rest, RBAC, secrets in a vault' boilerplate).

Nodes and routes are derived from dispatch in the graph definition, not inferred from the order of prose or function definitions, and the guide states whether the graph is framework-defined or prompt-orchestrated.
A source register exists recording path, version or revision, and freshness for the sources inspected, produced by scripts/source_register.py rather than hand-written.
The guide contains a limitations and verification section naming what was excluded, what is unknown, and what would invalidate the document.
scripts/verify_doc.py is run against the deliverable and its failures are addressed or reported.
No secrets, credentials or private endpoint values appear in the deliverable.
The file is written into docs/ without asking permission first, since it is a new file inside the authorized location.
Repair of any verification failure stops at two attempts for the same failure, with anything unresolved reported to the user rather than looped on.

evals.name: operator-facing-runbook-depth
evals.prompt: Our on-call rotation keeps getting paged for the nightly ingestion agent and nobody except me knows how to recover it. I need a system guide they can actually use at 3am — what it does, how to tell it's broken, what they're allowed to restart and what they must not touch. Code's in services/ingest/, the runbook fragments we have are in ops/notes.md, and there are traces in logs/ from last month's runs.
evals.expected_output: A guide oriented to an authorized operator: observability signals and blind spots, triage, safe start/stop/resume, prohibited actions, escalation, and explicit stop conditions — with behavior seen in traces labeled observed and its scope named, and behavior only declared in code kept distinct.
expectations: The operations section states prerequisites, permitted roles, safe start/stop/trigger procedures, and expected healthy output.
The guide names prohibited actions and explicit stop-and-escalate conditions, not just procedures.
Recovery covers retry, resume, rollback or restore, and escalation ownership.
Behavior demonstrated by the traces in logs/ is labeled observed and its scope, version or time window is named, including which paths the traces did not exercise.
Behavior read only from code or the notes file is labeled declared and is not presented as demonstrated.
The observability section names blind spots — what is not instrumented and will have to be detected by hand.
Conflicts between ops/notes.md and the code are surfaced as findings rather than silently resolved in favour of one.
The guide still covers the other required content areas rather than narrowing to a runbook, or states a reason for any area marked not applicable.
A diagram appears only where it answers a reader question prose would answer worse, and every visual carries a title, takeaway, scope, evidence status and a text equivalent.

evals.name: small-job-stays-cheap
evals.prompt: Quick one — can you document the little retry wrapper agent in tools/retry_agent.py? It's about 200 lines, one node, no deployment story, we run it locally. Just needs to be enough that someone else can pick it up.
evals.expected_output: A short but complete guide proportionate to a 200-line single-node local tool: applicable areas covered, inapplicable ones marked with reasons, and no assurance machinery beyond the default workflow.
expectations: Areas that genuinely do not apply (deployment topology, HA, observability infrastructure) are marked not applicable with a stated reason rather than padded with invented content.
Areas that do apply — node contract, state, configuration, failure and retry semantics, limitations — are covered with real detail from the file.
The retry and failure semantics are documented specifically, including bounds, since that is the entire subject of the tool.

No persisted claim registry, canonical JSON handoff artifact, approval gate for drafting, or multi-stage artifact chain is introduced — none of the escalation triggers apply and the run does not invent one.
No approval is requested before writing the new file.
The run does not spend tokens narrating bookkeeping that scripts/source_register.py performs.
A verification summary is still produced, however brief.

evals.name: update-patches-rather-than-regenerates
evals.prompt: The system doc at docs/system-guide.md is from three months ago. Since then we added a validation node with a repair loop back to the drafting node, swapped the summarizer model, and moved the checkpointer from memory to Postgres. Update it — don't rewrite the whole thing, the rest was reviewed and is fine.
evals.expected_output: A targeted update: changed sources identified by comparing registers, only affected sections and visuals revised, unaffected reviewed material preserved, stale claims removed rather than inherited, and a semantic diff presented before overwriting.
expectations: The run compares current sources against the previously recorded register (source_register.py --merge) rather than re-deriving everything from scratch.
Only the sections the changed evidence touches are revised — graph behavior, route contracts including the new repair back-edge and its bound, models and prompts, state persistence.
Reviewed sections whose evidence did not change are preserved rather than reworded.
Claims contradicted by the new evidence — in-memory checkpointing, the old summarizer model — are removed, not carried forward.
Only visuals affected by the change are re-rendered.
A concise semantic diff and its risks are presented to the user and approval is obtained before the existing file is overwritten.
The repair back-edge is documented with its trigger and its bound, not only the forward routes.
The freshness and verification section is updated to reflect the new inspection date and revision.
